paragraphs.heading: Matter circling a heavy object
paragraphs.text: An accretion disk is a structure made of diffuse material orbiting a massive central body, which is most often a star. Friction, uneven irradiance, magnetic effects in the gas and other forces cause instabilities that make the orbiting material spiral inward. Gravity and friction squeeze and heat the material until it gives off electromagnetic radiation. Which kind depends on the central object's mass: disks around young stars and protostars glow in the infrared, while those around neutron stars and black holes glow in X-rays.

paragraphs.heading: Why matter spirals in
paragraphs.text: Material entering the disk follows an inward spiral path. In the turbulent flow, particles rub and knock against one another, and the frictional heating radiates energy away and lowers their angular momentum. That loss shows up as a drop in speed, and a slower particle has to take a lower orbit. As it falls to that lower orbit, some of its gravitational potential energy becomes speed, so it ends up moving faster even though it has lost energy overall.

paragraphs.heading: Hot enough for X-rays
paragraphs.text: The closer a particle orbits, the faster it moves and the more friction heats it, as more of its potential energy is radiated away. Just outside the event horizon of a black hole, the disk is hot enough to give off X-rays. Accretion can turn about 10 percent to over 40 percent of an object's mass into energy, compared with around 0.7 percent for nuclear fusion. The great brightness of quasars is believed to come from gas being accreted by supermassive black holes.

paragraphs.heading: Disks all over the sky
paragraphs.text: Accretion disks show up everywhere in astrophysics: they are part of active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts and protoplanetary disks. The most prominent belong to active galactic nuclei and quasars, believed to be huge black holes sitting at the centres of galaxies. These disks very often launch jets from near the central object. Jets let the star-and-disk system shed angular momentum without losing too much mass.

paragraphs.heading: Disks between two stars
paragraphs.text: In a close pair of stars, the heavier star evolves faster and may already have become a black hole, a neutron star or a white dwarf when its lighter partner becomes a giant and overflows its Roche lobe. Gas then flows from the companion toward the heavier star. Conservation of angular momentum stops the gas from flowing straight across, so it forms an accretion disk instead.

paragraphs.heading: Where planets may begin
paragraphs.text: The disks that surround T Tauri or Herbig stars go by the name protoplanetary disks, because they are thought to be the forerunners of planetary systems. Here the gas being pulled in comes from the molecular cloud the star was born from, not from a companion star.

paragraphs.heading: Modelling the disk
paragraphs.text: Viscous stresses were clearly able to heat matter toward the centre, but viscosity by itself could not explain how angular momentum moves to the outer disk. Turbulence that boosts viscosity was thought to do this, though where the turbulence came from was not well understood. In 1973 Shakura and Sunyaev proposed turbulence in the gas as the source of the extra viscosity. The usual α-model describes that boost with one adjustable number, α. Many observable features depend only weakly on α, so the model still makes predictions. In 1991 the rediscovery of the magnetorotational instability showed that a weakly magnetized disk around a heavy, compact object would be highly unstable, giving a direct way to move angular momentum.
